1000266.etyen:
Borrowed from German Sauerkraut (“sauerkraut”), from sauer (“sour”) + Kraut (“herb; cabbage”), literally “sour cabbage”. German sauer continues Middle High German sūr (“sour”), from Old High German sūr, from Proto-Germanic *sūraz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *súHros (“sour”). German Kraut continues Middle High German krūt, from Old High German krūt, from Proto-West Germanic *krūd (“plant, vegetable, herb”). First attested in 1901 in Norwegian, in Lorentz Dietrichson’s Svundne Tider.
Compare Danish sauerkraut and Swedish sauerkraut (“sauerkraut”). Also compare surkål (“sour cabbage”), a

The name of the principal note takes the ending -ississ; for example, a double sharp on D becomes dississ, corresponding to E on the piano.

1005130.etyen:
From diss (“D-sharp”) + -iss (“semitone-raising suffix”), literally “D-sharp-sharp”. The base diss (“D-sharp”) is itself formed from d (“the note D”) and -iss (“semitone-raising suffix; sharp”); the latter is from German -is (“semitone-raising suffix; sharp”).
Compare the parallel formations Danish disis, Swedish dississ, German Disis, Dutch disis and Finnish disis (“D double sharp”).
